strengths: Novel and well-motivated idea: applying frequency-domain (DCT) compression to KV states of decoder-only LLMs is, to the authors' knowledge, unexplored, and the paper provides empirical evidence (Figure 1, Appendix A) that KV energy concentrates in low-frequency components across decoder layers and heads.

Simple and practical method: FreqKV requires no additional parameters or architectural changes, works for both fine-tuning and inference, and the iterative compression design keeps cache size bounded below the context window with negligible overhead (0.64% decoding latency, <0.04% FLOPs overhead at 32K).

Comprehensive evaluation: perplexity on PG-19 and Proof-pile at lengths up to 32K, LongBench across 14 tasks, and Needle-in-a-Haystack, with appropriate baselines (Full FT, LongLoRA, LoCoCo, LM-Infinite, LongHeads, SnapKV, PyramidKV) and reproduced baselines marked transparently.

Good empirical results: FreqKV beats LoCoCo on both LM and understanding tasks, is competitive with or better than full-cache LongLoRA on PG-19 despite a compressed cache, and achieves SOTA among KV-compression methods on LongBench for both LLaMA-2 and LLaMA-3.

Useful design analyses: the RoPE-before-compression vs. after-compression ablation (Appendix B) and the attention-mask design for iterative chunk-wise compression clarify important implementation choices; a training-free-style Dropping variant isolates the benefit of frequency compression (NIAH 84.2% vs 75.5%).
weaknesses: Theoretical justification is thin: why low-pass filtering (which essentially smooths the key/value sequences along the time dimension) preserves the information needed for precise token-level attention is not analyzed beyond the observed energy concentration; the claim of 'minimal information loss' is asserted from empirical PPL rather than a principled information-theoretic argument.

The core mechanism is a fairly straightforward application of DCT truncation plus sink tokens and sliding-window-style chunking, combining known ingredients (attention sinks [26], chunk-wise compression, RoPE position re-indexing), so the methodological novelty is moderate.

Comparison with full-cache methods (LongLoRA, Full FT) conflates two factors (compressed vs. full cache during inference), making the reported gains harder to attribute; a direct comparison at matched KV-cache memory budgets with other compression baselines (e.g., SnapKV/PyramidKV) on language modeling metrics is missing.

Ablations are limited: retaining ratio is studied only for base-model PPL on one dataset, and there is no sensitivity analysis for the number of sink tokens, chunking granularity, or behavior at very long lengths on downstream tasks; statistical rigor (seeds/variance) for the fine-tuning results is not reported.

Robustness concerns are under-explored: retrieval-heavy tasks requiring exact positional detail (e.g., some LongBench code/retrieval tasks show drops, e.g., LCC and Rep-P for LLaMA-3, MF-en for LLaMA-2) suggest possible failure modes that deserve more discussion; only 7B/8B models and two model families are tested.

strengths: Novel and clearly articulated idea: applying DCT-based low-pass filtering to the KV cache along the sequence dimension for decoder-only LLMs, claimed as the first frequency-domain KV compression method, with no additional parameters or architectural changes required.

Well-motivated empirical observation (Figure 1 and Appendix A) showing energy concentration in low-frequency components of key/value states across layers and heads, which directly supports the design.

Comprehensive evaluation: perplexity on PG-19 and Proof-pile at context lengths up to 32K, LongBench across five task categories, Needle-in-a-Haystack visualizations, comparisons against Full FT, LongLoRA, LoCoCo, LM-Infinite, LongHeads, SnapKV, and PyramidKV, with several baselines faithfully reproduced using official code.

Careful handling of practical details: attention sinks, RoPE applied before caching to avoid out-of-bound position embeddings (with an informative ablation in Appendix B), GQA compatibility for LLaMA-3, and amplitude rescaling after truncation.

Thorough efficiency analysis: decoding latency (Table 3, Figure 5) and FLOPs accounting (Table 5) demonstrate that compression overhead is negligible (<0.5%) and that memory/compute scale linearly rather than quadratically.
Useful ablations: retaining ratio (Figure 4) shows robustness across gamma values, and the iterative compression design is analyzed and justified.
weaknesses: The core insight—that signals concentrate energy in low-frequency components—is well-established in the CNN/signal-processing literature, and low-pass filtering is a fairly simple operation; the methodological novelty is incremental even if the application domain is new.

Uniform truncation of the top (1-gamma) frequency components is a blunt compression strategy; no adaptive or learned frequency selection is explored, and it is unclear how much headroom exists over this fixed scheme.
Potential error accumulation from iteratively recompressing already-compressed KV states (lossy-on-lossy) is not theoretically or empirically analyzed in depth.

Some comparisons may not be fully apples-to-apples: LongLoRA retains the full cache (better quality at higher memory cost), and the paper's PPL advantage over it on PG-19 does not carry over to Proof-pile; the disadvantage on structured/mathematical text is explained but not resolved.

Missing comparisons to several recent KV compression/merging baselines (e.g., CaM, D2O, adaptive merging methods cited in related work), and no evaluation on very long contexts (beyond 64K) or on models with other position encoding schemes.

Analysis of *why* frequency-domain compression preserves semantics (beyond energy concentration) is limited; the connection between attention behavior and frequency content of keys/values remains largely unexplored.
Only 7B/8B-scale models are tested; generalization to larger models or other architectures is not demonstrated.

strengths: The core idea is novel and well-motivated: to the best of the reviewer's knowledge, this is indeed the first work to compress the KV cache of decoder-only LLMs in the frequency domain, transferring an observation well established for CNNs/encoders (energy concentration in low-frequency components) to autoregressive LLMs.

The method is simple, parameter-free, and architecture-agnostic: no additional compression modules are required, and it applies uniformly to both fine-tuning and inference, which makes it practically attractive compared to LoCoCo or Activation Beacon.

Several thoughtful design decisions are well justified: keeping attention-sink tokens uncompressed, applying RoPE after compression so compressed keys remain within the position window (with a compelling ablation in Appendix B showing degradation when RoPE is applied first), and chunk-wise prefilled attention.

The evaluation is reasonably broad: perplexity on PG-19 and Proof-pile across 2K-32K contexts, LongBench across 5 task categories with multiple recent KV-compression baselines (SnapKV, PyramidKV, LM-Infinite, LongHeads), and Needle-in-a-Haystack up to 16K, plus a dedicated 'Dropping' control that isolates the benefit of frequency-domain compression over simple token dropping.

Efficiency is carefully quantified: decoding latency measurements and FLOPs analysis (Tables 3 and 5, Appendix D) show the compression overhead is negligible (<0.04% of FLOPs, ~0.64% of decoding time at 32K), and the linear-vs-quadratic decoding time comparison in Figure 5 supports the efficiency claims.

Ablations on the retaining ratio (Figure 4) and head-wise spectral analysis (Appendix A) provide useful insight, and the paper demonstrates substantial context extension (8K training to 64K evaluation, 16x extension).
weaknesses: Iterative lossy compression raises a potential error-compounding concern: earlier tokens undergo many successive compression steps (each losing high-frequency content), and the paper does not directly analyze how information degrades as a function of the number of compression rounds a token has experienced, only the indirect positional argument about recent tokens.

Some LongBench results are mixed and undercut the 'consistent improvement' claim: for LLaMA-2, FreqKV clearly loses on MF-en (31.2 vs. 35.3 for SnapKV) and TriviaQA (56.0 vs. 60.7), and for LLaMA-3 it trails the base model and PyramidKV on several QA tasks; a more balanced discussion of where frequency compression underperforms attention-score-based eviction is needed.

The evaluation is limited to LLaMA-2-7b and LLaMA-3-8b; there is no evidence of generality to other model families (e.g., models with different RoPE bases, sliding-window attention, or MLA), which weakens claims of broad applicability.

Modern, more comprehensive long-context benchmarks (e.g., RULER, InfiniteBench, Lost-in-the-Middle variants) are absent; Needle-in-a-Haystack alone is a weak stress test for retrieval-style capability at the claimed extension lengths.

The empirical observation of energy concentration is shown only on CNN/DailyMail samples for one model family; no theoretical or cross-model justification is given for why low-frequency retention should preserve attention-relevant information, and the layer-0 spectrum (energy increasing with frequency) is left largely unexplained.
No code release or reproducibility statement is mentioned in the main text, which is a notable omission given that several baselines were reproduced by the authors.

The comparison with LongLoRA on understanding tasks is incomplete (no LongLoRA LongBench numbers), so the claimed advantage over fine-tuning baselines on downstream tasks rests mainly on LM-Infinite/LongHeads reported numbers rather than direct comparisons.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated idea: this appears to be the first work to compress KV cache in the frequency domain (via DCT along the sequence dimension) for decoder-only LLMs, with a clear iterative compression scheme that preserves information of all tokens rather than evicting them.

Strong and extensive empirical validation: PG-19 and Proof-pile perplexity, LongBench, RULER, Needle-in-a-Haystack, and LongGenBench, with a broad set of baselines (SnapKV, PyramidKV, FastKV, ThinK, LaCache, D2O, CaM, KVMerger, LoCoCo, LongLoRA, Full FT) and comparison across LLaMA-2-7B/13B and LLaMA-3-8B.

The observation that FreqKV matches or exceeds Full FT perplexity while using a compressed cache, and generalizes from 8K training length to 256K evaluation with stable PPL, is a compelling headline result; training cost savings (~41% time, ~44% memory) further support practicality.

Good analysis of the mechanism: power spectrum analysis across layers/heads, a perturbation study showing low-frequency components encode robust global information, ablations on retaining ratio, sink size, rescaling, RoPE-before-compression variant, and a Dropping-variant control isolating the benefit of frequency-domain compression.

Careful engineering details are addressed: RoPE integration (compressing keys before RoPE avoids out-of-bound position embeddings), amplitude rescaling for iterative DCT/IDCT, negligible compression overhead (<0.4% FLOPs/latency), and code + supplementary material for reproducibility.
weaknesses: The method requires fine-tuning (LongLoRA-style LoRA + SFT on LongAlpaca) to adapt to compression, whereas several baselines (SnapKV, PyramidKV, FastKV, D2O) are training-free. A comparison of FreqKV without any fine-tuning would clarify how much of the advantage comes from frequency compression vs. adaptation training.

Repeated lossy compression of the same tokens (earlier tokens undergo many compression rounds) is central to the method, but error accumulation is only analyzed empirically; no theoretical or quantitative analysis of reconstruction error growth is provided. Applying DCT to a cache that mixes reconstructed (already-compressed) and incoming tokens is heuristic and lacks justification.

Performance still degrades substantially at 16K on RULER (avg 47.30 vs. 86.81 at 8K, e.g., NIAH drops to 25.47), which somewhat tempers the claim of robust context extension; the paper frames this mainly relative to total collapse of baselines rather than discussing the cause of FreqKV's own degradation.

Some results are counterintuitive and under-discussed: FreqKV's PPL beats Full FT (7.45 vs 7.55 at 2K), which likely reflects cache-size/attention effects and deserves deeper analysis; also FreqKV is not uniformly best on LongBench (e.g., code completion tasks, MF-en at 50% ratio).

Evaluation is limited to the LLaMA-2/LLaMA-3 model families (7B-13B); generalization to other architectures (e.g., Mistral, Qwen), larger models, or models with different RoPE/GQA configurations is untested.

Significant gains are concentrated on summarization/QA-style tasks; the uniform per-layer/per-head retaining ratio ignores the heterogeneity revealed by the head-wise spectrum analysis (Appendix B), suggesting an obvious extension that could strengthen the method but is left unexplored.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated angle: the observation that KV states exhibit energy concentration in low-frequency components (Figures 1-2), and the idea of compressing the KV cache via DCT/IDCT along the sequence dimension, is a fresh contribution to the KV compression literature for decoder-only LLMs.

The iterative compression scheme (Section 3.4) is elegant: it naturally allocates less compression to recent tokens and more to older ones, aligns well with autoregressive generation, and enables true context window extension rather than mere cache compression.

The RoPE handling (compressing key states before RoPE, re-allocating positions within the cache) is a thoughtful design choice that explains why FreqKV does not collapse beyond the pretrained window while eviction-based baselines do; the ablation in Appendix C substantiates this.

Extensive and multi-faceted evaluation: perplexity (PG-19, Proof-pile) up to 256K extrapolation, LongBench, RULER, Needle-in-a-Haystack, and LongGenBench, with many baselines reproduced and thorough ablations (retaining ratio, sink size, rescaling, high/low-frequency variants) in the appendix.

Impressive efficiency results: negligible compression overhead (<0.3% latency, <0.5% FLOPs), approximately linear decoding time, and reduced training cost/time relative to full fine-tuning (Table 7). Code is provided.
weaknesses: Unfair baseline comparison on the understanding benchmarks: FreqKV is fine-tuned (LongLoRA-style SFT on LongAlpaca) while nearly all LongBench/RULER baselines (SnapKV, PyramidKV, FastKV, D2O, GemFilter, LaCache, ThinK, KVMerger, CaM) are training-free methods applied to off-the-shelf instruct models. The central claim that FreqKV 'consistently outperforms existing KV compression methods' is therefore confounded by the extra fine-tuning. Fine-tuned competitors (e.g., Activation Beacon, Landmark attention) are largely absent from the LongBench/RULER/LongGenBench comparisons.

The claimed superiority is weaker than the text suggests: on LongBench, PyramidKV at a 1% retaining ratio (35.10 for LLaMA-2, 39.92 for LLaMA-3) nearly matches FreqKV at 1% (35.54, 42.81) and beats it on several tasks; on RULER at 8K, FreqKV's gains over PyramidKV/LLaMA-3 full cache are modest, and at 16K FreqKV degrades substantially (47.30 vs 86.81 in-window), so the practical benefit at extreme compression remains questionable.

Moderate novelty of the core ingredient: the low-frequency energy concentration of neural representations is well documented (Frequency Principle, FNet, Fourier Transformer), and DCT-based truncation is a standard signal-processing tool; the contribution is primarily in the engineering of the iterative cache pipeline rather than a new technical principle.

The 'parameter-free' framing is potentially misleading: while no additional modules are introduced, the method requires supervised fine-tuning of the model to function, which is a real cost and should be weighed against training-free alternatives more carefully.

Evaluation scope is limited to the LLaMA-2/LLaMA-3 model family; there is no evidence on modern long-context models, and no comparison with position-interpolation/LongRoPE-style extension combined with KV compression, which is the most natural competing recipe for window extension.
Possible train/test overlap concern: LongAlpaca (used for FreqKV's SFT) is related to the LongBench ecosystem; the paper does not discuss whether evaluation data overlaps with fine-tuning data.

Retrieval-heavy and exact-copy tasks suffer (RULER 16K: QA 34.00, NIAH 25.47; Proof-pile trails LongLoRA), which is expected since frequency truncation destroys token-identical information; the paper would benefit from a clearer analysis of when frequency compression is and is not appropriate.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated idea: the observation that KV states of LLMs exhibit energy concentration in low-frequency components (via DCT) is clearly demonstrated (Figure 1, perturbation study in Figure 2, summarization ablation in Table 1), and FreqKV is, to my knowledge, the first method to exploit frequency-domain compression of the KV cache for decoder-only autoregressive LLMs.

The method is simple, parameter-free, and architecture-agnostic, and the iterative compression design is well aligned with autoregressive decoding (recent tokens undergo fewer compressions). The handling of RoPE (compressing keys before position encoding to avoid out-of-bound positions) is a thoughtful and important design choice, supported by the ablation in Appendix C (Table 8).

Comprehensive and convincing evaluation: language modeling (PG-19, Proof-pile) vs. Full FT, LongLoRA, LoCoCo across 7B/13B and 8K/16K/32K training lengths; understanding (LongBench, RULER, Needle-in-a-Haystack) against a broad set of eviction-, merging-, and channel-compression baselines; and generation (LongGenBench). FreqKV consistently leads, and the 8K→256K extrapolation with stable perplexity (Table 6) is a striking result.

Strong efficiency analysis: compression overhead measured via FLOPs and wall-clock latency (<0.4% overhead, Table 13, Figure 8), training time/memory savings vs. Full FT (Table 7), and a clear explanation of linear-time decoding.

Thorough ablations in the appendix (high/low-frequency retention, retaining ratio including train/eval mismatch, sink size, rescaling factor, Dropping variant), which strengthen the empirical claims. Code is provided, and training/evaluation settings are sufficiently detailed for reproduction.
weaknesses: Fairness of comparisons: the KV-compression baselines on LongBench/RULER (SnapKV, PyramidKV, FastKV, D2O, etc.) are training-free inference-time methods, while FreqKV is fine-tuned on LongAlpaca; similarly, the RULER/Needle baseline collapse at 16K stems from out-of-bound position embeddings, which FreqKV avoids by design. The comparison is informative for context extension, but the paper should more carefully disentangle the gains from fine-tuning versus the compression mechanism itself (e.g., a training-free FreqKV variant or baselines given equivalent tuning).

Some results are difficult to interpret and raise questions: at 50% compression FreqKV outperforms the 100% Full Cache on several LongBench tasks (e.g., Qasper 41.6 vs. 31.83, MF-en 43.62 vs. 41.04, 2WikiMQA 40.54 vs. 36.68), which is surprising for a lossy compression method and deserves explanation (variance across runs? regularization effect of compression?). Error bars/significance tests are absent throughout.

The theoretical grounding is thin: the claim that low frequencies encode global semantics and high frequencies encode local details is supported empirically, but there is no analysis of why discarding high-frequency components preserves attention-relevant information, and the degradation at 16K on RULER (Avg. 47.30 vs. 86.81 at 8K, particularly NIAH dropping to 25.47) suggests the method does lose needle-like local information — the limitations here should be discussed more candidly.

Scope is limited to LLaMA-2/LLaMA-3 family models up to 13B; generalization to other architectures (e.g., sliding-window or hybrid attention models) and much larger scales is untested. The RoPE-centric design may not transfer directly to other positional encodings.

Minor clarity issues: the paper claims 'parameter-free' but requires LoRA fine-tuning to adapt to the compression; notation in Eq. (3)-(5) (superscript/subscript ranges for iteratively re-compressed caches) is hard to follow; the LongBench table is dense and hard to parse.
